questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Three tissue systems in a vascular plant
questions.learningObjective: Identify the three tissue systems of a vascular plant and their main functions
questions.stem: A software team's ticket asks which three tissue systems make up a typical vascular plant and how they divide the work of transport and support.

options.text: Dermal, ground and vascular tissue, with vascular tissue handling transport.
Protective, photosynthetic and vascular tissue, split by the cell type found.
options.misconception: confuses tissue systems with cell types

options.text: Epidermal, mesophyll and cambium tissue, ordered from outside the stem inward.
options.misconception: lists layers of one organ as whole-organ systems

options.text: Roots, stems and leaves, treated as three distinct tissue systems.
options.misconception: confuses organs with tissue systems

questions.explanation: Dermal, ground and vascular tissue form the three systems. The other choices confuse tissue systems with cell types or with whole organs such as roots, stems and leaves.
questions.hint: Think outer sheet, filling, and plumbing.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Xylem and phloem as separate conduits
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the transport route of xylem from that of phloem
questions.stem: Another ticket asks the team to state which direction each vascular conduit carries material in a growing plant.

options.text: Xylem moves sugars upward; phloem moves water and minerals upward.
options.misconception: reverses the transport role of each conduit

options.text: Xylem moves water and minerals upward; phloem moves sugars from sources to sinks.
Both conduits move water upward, but only xylem moves dissolved sugars.
options.misconception: assumes both conduits transport the same cargo

options.text: Xylem carries water downward and phloem carries sugars upward.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of xylem water flow

questions.explanation: Xylem conducts water and minerals upward, while phloem carries sucrose from sources to sinks. Swapping the cargo or reversing xylem flow contradicts how each tissue is built.
questions.hint: Water goes up one tube, sugar goes wherever it is needed.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Vascular bundles: ring versus scattered arrangement
questions.learningObjective: Use a cross-section sketch to tell a ring arrangement from a scattered one
questions.stem: One ticket includes a stem cross-section sketch in which vascular bundles form a single unbroken circle just inside the surface; identify the arrangement and the likely plant group.

options.text: Bundles scattered through the ground tissue, which is the dicot condition.
options.misconception: confuses scattered bundles with the ring condition

options.text: Bundles in a ring, but only because the stem is a monocot with a hollow centre.
options.misconception: links the ring arrangement to monocot stems

options.text: Bundles in a ring, characteristic of a dicot stem with secondary growth potential.
Bundles scattered in two concentric rings, indicating a monocot stem.
options.misconception: invents a two-ring arrangement not present in the sketch

questions.explanation: A continuous circle of bundles just inside the epidermis indicates a dicot stem, where a cambium can link the bundles. Scattered bundles are the monocot condition.
questions.hint: Look for one unbroken circle just inside the epidermis.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Monocot and dicot comparison
questions.learningObjective: Match a labelled stem section to monocot or dicot anatomy
questions.stem: A second ticket contains a labelled stem section showing scattered vascular bundles with no visible vascular cambium ring; label the group this section represents.

options.text: A dicot, because scattered bundles appear only where secondary growth stops.
options.misconception: reverses which group has scattered vascular bundles

options.text: A dicot, because a missing cambium ring means the bundles cannot merge.
options.misconception: assumes cambium loss is proof of dicot identity

options.text: A monocot, because monocot stems always lack a defined ground tissue layer.
options.misconception: claims monocots lack ground tissue between bundles

options.text: A monocot, since scattered bundles and absent cambium are typical monocot features.

questions.explanation: Scattered bundles with no cambium ring mark a monocot stem, since monocot bundles stay closed. The distractors invert the group labels or invent rules about ground tissue and cambium that do not hold.
questions.hint: Closed scattered bundles mean no secondary growth.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Root cap protection at the tip
questions.learningObjective: Find the flawed step in a described method of protecting a root tip
questions.stem: The ticket proposes that technicians remove a plant's root cap each week to let the root tip reach deeper soil, then record growth; identify the fault.

options.text: Removing the cap exposes the root tip to abrasion and pathogen entry, so growth data are unsafe.
Removing the cap is standard practice and simply speeds up the root tip lengthening.
options.misconception: assumes the root cap inhibits elongation

options.text: The fault is that weekly removal is too frequent; removing it once a season would be correct.
options.misconception: blames the frequency of removal instead of removal itself

options.text: The fault is that the technicians should also water more often while the cap is absent.
options.misconception: redirects the fault to watering, ignoring cap function

questions.explanation: The root cap shields the apical meristem from abrasion and pathogens, so removing it endangers the tip. Blaming timing or watering overlooks that protective role entirely.
questions.hint: Ask what the cap is there to protect.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Root hairs and absorption surface area
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total absorptive surface contributed by a zone of root hairs
questions.stem: A software team's ticket reports that a 10 mm zone of root bears root hairs spaced 24 per millimetre, and each hair adds 0.10 square millimetres of surface; what total hair surface area does the zone provide?
questions.explanation: The zone holds 24 hairs per millimetre over 10 mm, giving 240 hairs, and 240 multiplied by 0.10 mm² per hair gives 24 mm². Forgetting to multiply by the zone length understates the total.
questions.hint: Density times length gives count; then count times area.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Water potential and its two components
questions.learningObjective: Calculate total water potential from solute and pressure potentials
questions.stem: A third ticket gives a root cell with a solute potential of -0.4 MPa and a pressure potential of +0.3 MPa; what is the cell's total water potential in MPa?
questions.explanation: Total water potential is the sum of solute and pressure potentials, so -0.4 plus 0.3 gives -0.1 MPa. Treating the two components as alternatives, or ignoring pressure, would give an incorrect total.
questions.hint: Water potential adds solute and pressure potentials.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Solute potential from molarity
questions.learningObjective: Explain how solute concentration determines the solute potential of a solution
questions.stem: One question asks the team to explain, in writing, why a cell with a higher internal solute concentration holds more water than a cell with a lower one.

answer.exemplar: A higher solute concentration lowers the solute potential, so the water potential of the cell becomes more negative. Because water moves from higher to lower water potential, water flows into the more concentrated cell by osmosis, causing it to swell until pressure potential rises and balances the difference.

questions.explanation: The answer must link solute concentration to solute potential, then to total water potential, then to osmosis direction. A response stopping at says solute pulls water misses the potential terms.
questions.hint: Explain the chain: concentration to potential to flow.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Three tissue systems in a vascular plant
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of which tissue system carries water in a cut stem
questions.stem: A fourth ticket asks the team to design an experiment that shows which tissue system carries the water taken up by a cut stem.

answer.exemplar: Take two similar leafy shoots with identical root systems and place each in a beaker of coloured water with the stem cut at the base. Leave them for the same period, then section the stem and examine the path of colour in transverse and longitudinal slices. Colour confined to the xylem shows that xylem, not phloem, carries water and dissolved minerals upward, and controls without colour confirm the result is due to uptake.

questions.explanation: A valid design needs a tracer, matched shoots and a time control, then checks where the colour sits. Adding dye only to leaves, or omitting the comparison, fails to isolate the conducting tissue.
questions.hint: Use a tracer and compare where it ends up.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Xylem and phloem as separate conduits
questions.learningObjective: Combine a conduit-identification step with a transport-direction step
questions.stem: A fifth ticket asks which vascular tissue in a woody stem carries sucrose upward from a mature leaf, and in which direction the xylem moves water.

options.text: Xylem carries the sucrose upward; phloem moves water down toward the roots.
options.misconception: swaps the cargo carried by xylem and phloem

options.text: Phloem carries the sucrose; xylem moves water upward toward the leaves.
Phloem carries the sucrose; xylem moves water downward from leaves to roots.
options.misconception: reverses the xylem water flow direction

options.text: Xylem carries the sucrose and water together in the same vessel element.
options.misconception: claims one conduit carries both sugar and water

questions.explanation: Sugar made in a leaf is exported by phloem sieve tubes toward sinks, and xylem water moves upward under transpiration pull. The wrong options either swap the conduits or reverse the water flow.
questions.hint: Sugar travels on its own tube; water climbs another.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Vascular bundles: ring versus scattered arrangement
questions.learningObjective: Relate bundle arrangement to a stem's capacity for secondary growth
questions.stem: A later ticket asks how the vascular bundle arrangement of a stem relates to the plant's capacity for secondary growth.

options.text: Ring-arranged bundles block any cambium from forming between them.
options.misconception: thinks bundle crowding prevents cambium formation

options.text: Scattered bundles always merge into a cambium that makes secondary tissue.
options.misconception: claims scattered bundles always fuse into cambium

options.text: Ring-arranged bundles can be joined by a cambium, so secondary growth is possible.
Both arrangements grow alike, since bundle position never affects thickening.
options.misconception: denies any link between arrangement and thickening

questions.explanation: Dicot stems with ring-arranged bundles can form a vascular cambium that links them and adds secondary tissue. The distractors claim crowding blocks cambium or that scattered bundles fuse.
questions.hint: Think about what cambium needs to connect.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Monocot and dicot comparison
questions.learningObjective: Select features that separate a monocot stem from a dicot stem
questions.stem: Another question asks which pair of features reliably separates a monocot stem from a dicot stem in a young plant.

options.text: Thick bark and secondary xylem indicate a monocot; thin bark indicates a dicot.
options.misconception: uses bark thickness to classify stems

options.text: Parallel leaf veins and a fibrous root system indicate a dicot rather than a monocot.
options.misconception: reverses the meaning of parallel veins and fibrous roots

options.text: One seed leaf in the embryo indicates a monocot; two seed leaves indicate a dicot.
options.misconception: reverses the one-versus-two cotyledon rule

options.text: Scattered bundles and absent cambium indicate a monocot; ring bundles indicate a dicot.

questions.explanation: Monocot stems show scattered closed bundles; dicot stems show a ring of bundles with room for cambium. Bark thickness and venation are unreliable for stems, and the cotyledon rule has been reversed.
questions.hint: Scattered and closed, versus a ring that can connect.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Root cap protection at the tip
questions.learningObjective: Identify a shedding layer at the root tip from micrograph evidence
questions.stem: One ticket includes micrographs of a root tip where the outermost cell layer is sloughing off and cells beneath are dividing actively; identify that layer.

options.text: The root cap, whose outer cells are shed to protect the apical meristem.
The epidermis of the root, which matures and then flakes away as the root grows.
options.misconception: confuses the sloughing layer with the mature epidermis

options.text: The cortex, whose cells die back as the root thickens through secondary growth.
options.misconception: attributes shedding to secondary thickening of the cortex

options.text: The endodermis, which sheds cells as the stele expands after cambium forms.
options.misconception: confuses the endodermis with a protective cap at the tip

questions.explanation: Shedding outer cells over dividing cells identify the root cap, whose wear layer replaces itself continually. The mature epidermis does not flake, and cortex shedding is not a tip feature.
questions.hint: The cap is a sacrificial layer that rubs away.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Root hairs and absorption surface area
questions.learningObjective: Name a root outgrowth and state its function from micrograph evidence
questions.stem: A ticket shows a labelled micrograph of a root surface where long single-cell outgrowths project from epidermal cells; name the structure and its main job.

options.text: Root cap cells, which secrete mucilage to lubricate the tip as it pushes through soil.
options.misconception: confuses absorptive hairs with the lubricating root cap

options.text: Root hairs, which increase the absorptive surface area in contact with soil water.
Lateral roots, which branch outward to reach patches of water deeper in the profile.
options.misconception: confuses root hairs with lateral root branches

options.text: Root nodules, where bacteria fix nitrogen for the plant in exchange for sugars.
options.misconception: confuses root hairs with nitrogen-fixing nodules

questions.explanation: Long single-cell projections from epidermal cells are root hairs, multiplying the surface available for water and ion uptake. A cap, lateral root and nodule are separate structures.
questions.hint: Single cells, not branches, that boost uptake area.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Water potential and its two components
questions.learningObjective: Find the sign error in a reported water potential calculation
questions.stem: One spreadsheet shows a cell's water potential was computed by subtracting its pressure potential from its solute potential; find the error.

options.text: The calculation is right, but the units should be reported in kPa rather than megapascals.
options.misconception: blames unit choice rather than the sign rule

options.text: The calculation is right, but pressure potential should be treated as zero in every cell.
options.misconception: assumes pressure potential is always zero in cells

options.text: The calculation is wrong; water potential is the sum of solute and pressure potentials.
The calculation is right, but solute potential must be made positive before it is used.
options.misconception: insists solute potential must be positive to be used

questions.explanation: Water potential equals solute potential plus pressure potential, so subtracting is wrong. Unit conversion and forcing a positive solute potential are separate issues, and pressure is rarely zero.
questions.hint: Add the two components, do not subtract them.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Solute potential from molarity
questions.learningObjective: Calculate solute potential from molarity, a constant and a temperature
questions.stem: A calculation asks for the solute potential of a 0.50 mol per litre solution using the constant 0.0082 litres of megapascals per mole per kelvin at a temperature of 300 kelvin; what value in megapascals results?
questions.explanation: Solute potential is minus molarity times the constant times temperature, so -0.50 times 0.0082 times 300 gives -1.23 MPa. Dropping the temperature or the sign gives a wrong magnitude.
questions.hint: Molarity times constant times temperature, then negate.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Three tissue systems in a vascular plant
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage surface gain produced by root hairs
questions.stem: A measurement states that a young root has a surface area of 40 square millimetres without root hairs and 220 square millimetres with them; what percentage increase do the hairs produce?
questions.explanation: The hairs add 220 minus 40 equals 180 square millimetres, and 180 divided by 40 gives 4.5, or 450 percent. Dividing the increase by the larger figure would understate the gain.
questions.hint: Increase over the original, not over the new total.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Xylem and phloem as separate conduits
questions.learningObjective: Explain why xylem and phloem must operate as separate conduits
questions.stem: One prompt asks the team to write about why plants need xylem and phloem to be separate conducting tissues rather than one shared tube.

answer.exemplar: Xylem and phloem carry materials in opposite directions and under different driving forces. Xylem transports water and minerals upward through dead, narrow, lignified conduits driven by transpiration pull, while phloem carries sucrose in living sieve tubes driven by pressure differences between source and sink. A single tube could not sustain both flows, since sugar solution moving one way would obstruct the water column needed to move the other way.

questions.explanation: The answer must show that the two conduits carry different cargo, directions and mechanisms. A reply that only says they are different tissues, without the flow argument, misses the contrast.
questions.hint: Compare cargo, direction and driving force.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Vascular bundles: ring versus scattered arrangement
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of bundle arrangements in monocot and dicot stems
questions.stem: A comparison asks the team to design a comparison that reveals how vascular bundles are arranged in a monocot stem against a dicot stem.

answer.exemplar: Take thin transverse sections from a comparable monocot stem and a dicot stem, stain them with a dye that binds lignin in the xylem, and mount them on slides. Under a low-power microscope, mark out the position of each stained bundle relative to the edge of the section. Record whether the bundles form an unbroken ring or are spread across the ground tissue, and repeat on several individuals of each type to avoid relying on a single section.

questions.explanation: The design needs comparable sections, a stain that shows bundles, a positional measurement and replication. Describing stems from memory cannot establish the arrangement.
questions.hint: Same stain, same magnification, several specimens each.

questions.topic: Monocot and dicot comparison
questions.learningObjective: Match leaf venation and root pattern to the correct plant group
questions.stem: A field question asks which leaf venation and root pattern a plant with scattered stem bundles would most likely show, and why the two fit together.

options.text: Netted leaf veins with a taproot, since both suit the dicot growth pattern.
options.misconception: pairs monocot stem anatomy with dicot organs

options.text: Parallel leaf veins with a taproot, matching a monocot stem and a dicot root.
options.misconception: mixes parallel veins with a taproot system

options.text: Netted leaf veins with a fibrous root system, matching the dicot stem shown.
options.misconception: mixes netted veins with a fibrous root system

options.text: Parallel leaf veins with a fibrous root system, since both suit the monocot growth pattern.

questions.explanation: Scattered stem bundles indicate a monocot, and monocots have parallel leaf venation and a fibrous root system. The wrong options pair these with dicot organs or with each other.
questions.hint: Monocot stems go with parallel veins and fibrous roots.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Root cap protection at the tip
questions.learningObjective: Identify the structure that shields the root apical meristem
questions.stem: A fresh ticket asks what structure actually protects the delicate root apical meristem as the root pushes through coarse soil.

options.text: A cap of parenchyma cells that continually slough off and are replaced from behind.
A sleeve of endodermal cells that stays intact and seals the meristem from soil.
options.misconception: thinks the endodermis caps the meristem

options.text: A layer of root hairs that cushions the tip and screens it from abrasive grains.
options.misconception: credits root hairs with tip protection

options.text: A sheath of sclerenchyma fibres that hardens the tip so it can bore through rock.
options.misconception: credits fibres with protecting a delicate meristem

questions.explanation: The root cap is a sacrificial parenchyma layer that wears away outside and is renewed inside, shielding the meristem. An endodermal seal, root hairs and a fibre sheath do not do that.
questions.hint: It wears away and is continuously replaced.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Root hairs and absorption surface area
questions.learningObjective: Explain why more root hairs matter more than thicker root hairs
questions.stem: Another question asks why enlarging the zone of root hairs matters more than thickening individual hairs.

options.text: Thicker hairs absorb faster because more cell wall touches the soil water directly.
options.misconception: thinks hair width is the only factor in uptake

options.text: More hairs spread over a length of root multiply the absorbing area without extra cost.
Root hairs only work in dry soil, so lengthening the zone has no effect there.
options.misconception: assumes root hairs function only in dry soils

options.text: Hairs absorb minerals only, so the total area says nothing about water uptake.
options.misconception: restricts root hairs to mineral uptake alone

questions.explanation: Absorption scales with total surface in contact with soil solution, so more hairs over more root length add area thicker hairs cannot. Width alone, dryness and mineral-only uptake are false limits.
questions.hint: What matters is the total area in contact with soil.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Water potential and its two components
questions.learningObjective: Compare two cells by their total water potential
questions.stem: One table tabulates two root cells: one with solute potential -0.5 MPa and pressure potential 0.2 MPa, another with solute potential -0.9 MPa and pressure potential 0.1 MPa; which takes in water more readily?

options.text: The first cell, since -0.5 plus 0.2 gives -0.3 MPa against -0.8 MPa for the second.
options.misconception: adds the potentials but compares them the wrong way round

options.text: Neither, because the two cells have the same solute concentration by mass alone.
options.misconception: ignores that solute concentration sets the water potential

options.text: The second cell, since -0.9 plus 0.1 gives -0.8 MPa against -0.3 MPa for the first.
Both equally, since uptake depends only on pressure potential and ignores solutes.
options.misconception: believes uptake depends only on pressure potential

questions.explanation: Total water potentials are -0.3 MPa and -0.8 MPa, so the second cell has the lower potential and draws water in. The comparison must add both components, not judge by one.
questions.hint: Add both components before comparing the two cells.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Solute potential from molarity
questions.learningObjective: Predict the shape of a solute potential against molarity graph
questions.stem: A graph plots solute potential against molarity for a sucrose solution at constant temperature; what shape should the line take?

options.text: A straight line through the origin with a positive slope, since more solute raises potential.
options.misconception: thinks added solute raises the solute potential

options.text: A curve that flattens as molarity rises, since the effect saturates at high concentration.
options.misconception: assumes solute potential saturates with concentration

options.text: A vertical line, because molarity cannot be varied without changing the temperature.
options.misconception: ties the relation to temperature rather than concentration

options.text: A straight line through the origin with a negative slope, since potential is proportional to molarity.

questions.explanation: Solute potential is directly proportional to molarity at fixed temperature, so the plot is a straight line of negative slope through the origin. A positive or saturating curve contradicts this.
questions.hint: Proportional means a straight line, and solutes pull down.

questions.topic: Three tissue systems in a vascular plant
questions.learningObjective: Correct a faulty definition of vascular tissue based on bark
questions.stem: One report states that a shoot's vascular tissue was scored as the total area of bark, phloem and cambium; find the fault in that definition.

options.text: Bark includes phloem and cambium but not xylem, so the score misses the conducting wood.
Bark equals the vascular tissue exactly, so the scoring method is sound as written.
options.misconception: accepts bark as a synonym for vascular tissue

options.text: The fault is that vascular tissue should be scored on length rather than on area.
options.misconception: blames area versus length instead of the missing xylem

options.text: The fault is that the cambium is vascular tissue and should be excluded from the score.
options.misconception: calls cambium vascular and recommends excluding it

questions.explanation: Bark covers everything outside the vascular cambium, which includes phloem but excludes the xylem inside it. Scoring bark as vascular tissue therefore misses the wood that carries water.
questions.hint: Bark is everything outside the cambium, not the wood.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total length of conducting tissue from counts and mean lengths
questions.stem: A count records 40 xylem vessels averaging 2 millimetres long and 35 sieve tubes averaging 1.5 millimetres long in one stem section; what total length of conducting tissue in millimetres is present?
questions.explanation: The vessels contribute 40 times 2 equals 80 millimetres and the sieve tubes 35 times 1.5 equals 52.5 millimetres, giving 132.5 in total. Averaging the two counts first would not weight them correctly.
questions.hint: Add each group's count times its own mean length.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the fraction of a stem circumference occupied by vascular bundles
questions.stem: A sketch shows a stem cross-section whose vascular bundles form a ring around 5 mm of circumference, each bundle 0.4 mm wide; what fraction of the circumference do the bundles occupy?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Monocot and dicot comparison
questions.learningObjective: Explain how bundle arrangement predicts the growth in thickness of a stem
questions.stem: A written account is requested of how a stem's vascular bundle arrangement predicts the way the plant will grow in thickness.

answer.exemplar: A ring of vascular bundles in a dicot stem leaves cambium tissue between neighbouring bundles that can connect into a continuous ring, allowing secondary xylem and phloem to be added and the stem to thicken. Scattered bundles in a monocot stem are usually closed, so there is no continuous cambium and the stem widens mainly by cell enlargement instead of secondary tissue.

questions.explanation: The answer must connect bundle position to a continuous cambium, and then to adding secondary tissue. Saying only that dicots thicken and monocots do not skips the cambium step entirely.
questions.hint: Cambium continuity is the link between layout and thickness.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Root cap protection at the tip
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of whether the root cap protects the apical meristem
questions.stem: A study asks the team to design an experiment that tests whether the root cap really protects the growing tip of the root.

answer.exemplar: Grow a matched set of seedlings with the same substrate and watering regime. Remove the root cap from half of them with fine forceps without disturbing the tip itself, and leave the other half untouched as controls. Track tip survival, meristem staining and new root length over the next two weeks. If capped and uncapped roots differ in damage and elongation, the cap protects the meristem; if the two groups are indistinguishable, the effect is not supported.

questions.explanation: The design needs matched plants, an untreated control, a measured outcome and a time course. Removing the meristem instead of the cap, or leaving out the control, would not test protection.
questions.hint: Matched plants, one group altered, one untouched.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Root hairs and absorption surface area
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the extra absorbing surface gained from a stated number of root hairs
questions.stem: A calculation asks how much extra absorbing surface a root gains from adding 300 root hairs of 0.15 square millimetres each, and where that surface sits.

questions.stem: One question asks for a written explanation of the mechanism by which root hairs improve water and mineral uptake.

answer.exemplar: Root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells that project into the soil, so thousands of them add a large surface area in contact with soil solution without producing much tissue. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Solute potential from molarity
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a solute solution has a lower water potential than pure water
questions.stem: A further question asks for a written explanation of why dissolved solute lowers the water potential of a solution.

answer.exemplar: Dissolved solute molecules are drawn onto the water molecules around them, reducing the fraction of water molecules that are free to move and to exchange with the vapour above the solution. Because fewer water molecules can move freely, the chemical potential of the water falls and the solution develops a negative solute potential. Pure water, with no solute to restrain its molecules, sits at zero potential by definition.

questions.explanation: The answer must link dissolved particles to reduced freedom of the water molecules and then to a lower chemical potential. Saying only that solute attracts water stops short of the potential change.
questions.hint: Fewer free water molecules means lower potential.

answer.exemplar: Xylem vessels are long tubes stacked end to end, with their end walls perforated or absent, so water meets almost no barrier as it travels upward. Their walls are thickened and lignified, which resists the collapse that the strong tension in the column would otherwise cause. The tubes are dead and empty at maturity, so there are no living membranes or organelles in the way of the flow, and the narrow lumen helps the column resist breaking.

answer.exemplar: Select a young dicot with ring-arranged bundles and a young monocot with scattered bundles of similar age and size, then grow them for one season under identical light, water and nutrients. At the start and end, measure stem circumference, count the xylem layers in a transverse section and record whether a continuous cambium ring formed. If the dicot thickens and adds xylem layers while the monocot mainly enlarges cells, the arrangement explains the difference.

questions.explanation: The investigation needs matched plants, controlled conditions, before-and-after measurement and a cambium check. Comparing a mature dicot with a seedling monocot confounds age.
questions.hint: Same age, same conditions, measure before and after.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Monocot and dicot comparison
questions.learningObjective: Select a venation and root pairing for a plant to be identified as a dicot
questions.stem: A final ticket asks a grower to choose a leaf venation and root system for a plant that will be identified as a dicot later.

options.text: Parallel leaf veins with a fibrous root system, matching the dicot pattern expected.
options.misconception: gives the dicot label to the monocot pair of features

options.text: Parallel leaf veins with a taproot, since the two patterns can be mixed freely.
options.misconception: believes venation and root pattern can be paired freely

options.text: Netted leaf veins with a fibrous root system, since only the venation shows in the field.
options.misconception: believes root pattern never helps identify the group

options.text: Netted leaf veins with a taproot, matching the dicot pattern the grower expects.

questions.explanation: Dicots show netted venation with a taproot, so that pair matches the expected identification. The options label the monocot pair as dicot, mix the features, or dismiss a character.
questions.hint: Pick the pair that always travels together.
